questions.subject: GRE Format
questions.q: How many Analytical Writing tasks are on the current (shorter) GRE General Test?
questions.e: The current GRE has one AWA task — Analyze an Issue (30 minutes). The Argument task was removed in September 2023.

questions.subject: GRE Format
questions.q: What is the total testing time of the current GRE General Test?
questions.e: The shorter GRE (since September 2023) takes about 1 hour 58 minutes, down from nearly 4 hours.

questions.subject: GRE Format
questions.q: How are the Verbal Reasoning and Quantitative Reasoning sections scored?
questions.e: Each measure is reported on a 130–170 scale in 1-point increments.

questions.subject: GRE Format
questions.q: How is the Analytical Writing measure scored?
questions.e: AWA is scored 0–6 in half-point increments by one human reader and one automated engine.

questions.subject: GRE Format
questions.q: How does section-level adaptivity work on the GRE?
o: Your first section's performance determines the difficulty of your second section in that measure
Every question gets harder as you answer correctly
Only the essay adapts to your writing level
The test is not adaptive at all
questions.e: The GRE is section-level adaptive: performance on the first Verbal/Quant section decides whether the second section is easier or harder. A harder second section unlocks higher scores.

questions.subject: GRE Format
questions.q: Is there a penalty for wrong answers on the GRE?
o: Yes, 1/4 point off per wrong answer
No — never leave a question blank
questions.e: There is no guessing penalty on the GRE. Always answer every question — eliminate choices, then guess.

questions.subject: GRE Format
questions.q: How long are GRE scores valid?
questions.e: GRE scores are valid for 5 years from the test date.

questions.subject: GRE Format
questions.q: What does ScoreSelect allow you to do?
o: Send only your best set of GRE scores to schools
questions.e: ScoreSelect lets you choose which test administration's scores to send to each institution.

questions.subject: GRE Format
questions.q: How many Verbal Reasoning questions appear in total on the GRE, and in how much time?
questions.e: Verbal: 2 sections, 27 questions total — 12 in 18 minutes, then 15 in 23 minutes (41 minutes total).

questions.subject: GRE Format
questions.q: How many Quantitative Reasoning questions appear in total on the GRE, and in how much time?
questions.e: Quant: 2 sections, 27 questions total — 12 in 21 minutes, then 15 in 26 minutes (47 minutes total).

questions.subject: GRE Format
questions.q: Which of these is provided during the Quantitative Reasoning sections?
o: A scientific calculator you must bring
questions.e: The GRE provides an on-screen calculator for the Quant sections. Personal calculators are not allowed.

questions.subject: GRE Format
questions.q: Approximately how much does the GRE General Test cost in most countries?
questions.e: The fee is about US$220 in most countries, though it varies by location — confirm the exact fee on ets.org when you register.

questions.subject: GRE Format
questions.q: Which statement about the current GRE format is TRUE?
o: There is an unscored experimental section
The Argument essay is still required
The test can be taken at home or at a test centre
Verbal sections come before the essay
questions.e: The GRE is offered both at test centres and as an at-home online test. There is no experimental section, and the essay (always first) is the Issue task only.

questions.subject: GRE Format
questions.q: Roughly what fraction of a Verbal section is Reading Comprehension?
questions.e: About half of each Verbal section (roughly 13 of 27 questions) is Reading Comprehension; the rest is Text Completion and Sentence Equivalence.

questions.subject: GRE Format
questions.q: Why does the FIRST section of each measure matter most under section-level adaptivity?
o: It determines your second section's difficulty, which caps your score range
Scores from it are reported separately
questions.e: Only a strong first section routes you to the harder second section, which is the only path to the top of the 130–170 scale. Protect accuracy early.

questions.subject: Text Completion
questions.q: The professor's lecture was so _____ that even the most diligent students struggled to stay awake.
questions.e: The clue 'struggled to stay awake' demands a word meaning sleep-inducing: soporific.

questions.subject: Text Completion
questions.q: Despite her _____ demeanor in meetings, she was known among friends for her warmth and humor.
questions.e: 'Despite' signals contrast with 'warmth and humor' — her meeting demeanor was the opposite: austere (stern, severe).

questions.subject: Text Completion
questions.q: The scientist's findings were initially met with _____, but later experiments confirmed their validity.
questions.e: 'But later experiments confirmed' contrasts with the initial reaction — skepticism (doubt) fits; acclaim/enthusiasm would agree with confirmation.

questions.subject: Text Completion
questions.q: His argument was so _____ that even his opponents conceded its logic.
questions.e: 'Even his opponents conceded' requires a strongly positive word for the argument: cogent (clear, logical, convincing).

questions.subject: Text Completion
questions.q: The novel's plot was predictable and _____, offering nothing that seasoned readers had not seen before.
questions.e: 'Predictable' and 'nothing... not seen before' demand a word meaning unoriginal: hackneyed.

questions.subject: Text Completion
questions.q: Far from being _____, the mayor's speech was a masterclass in evasive political rhetoric.
questions.e: 'Far from being' + 'evasive' sets up a contrast: the speech was not candid (frank, straightforward).

questions.subject: Text Completion
questions.q: The committee's report was exhaustive yet _____, covering every detail without ever reaching a conclusion.
questions.e: 'Without ever reaching a conclusion' directly defines the blank: inconclusive.

questions.subject: Text Completion
questions.q: Her _____ approach to research — checking every source twice — made her papers unusually reliable.
questions.e: The dash defines the approach: 'checking every source twice' = meticulous (showing great attention to detail).

questions.subject: Text Completion
questions.q: The dictator's _____ grip on power left no room for dissent or debate.
questions.e: 'Left no room for dissent' requires a firm, holding-fast grip: tenacious. (Tenuous means weak — a trap.)

questions.subject: Text Completion
questions.q: The once _____ neighborhood has become fashionable, with galleries replacing the old warehouses.
questions.e: 'Once' + 'has become fashionable' signals the neighborhood changed from the opposite state: derelict (in poor condition, neglected).

questions.subject: Text Completion
questions.q: His apology was so _____ that it only deepened the sense of grievance among those he had wronged.
questions.e: 'Only deepened the sense of grievance' shows the apology failed — it was perfunctory (done with minimum effort, half-hearted).

questions.subject: Text Completion
questions.q: The economist's predictions, though _____ at first, proved remarkably accurate over the following decade.
questions.e: 'Though... at first' + 'proved remarkably accurate' signals contrast: the predictions were initially derided (mocked).

questions.subject: Text Completion
questions.q: She approached the negotiations with a _____ that disarmed even the most hostile delegates.
questions.e: 'Disarmed even the most hostile delegates' requires a strikingly generous quality: magnanimity (generosity of spirit).

questions.subject: Text Completion
questions.q: The manuscript's _____ prose — dense with allusions and subordinate clauses — demanded a patient reader.
questions.e: The dash defines it: 'dense with allusions and subordinate clauses' = turgid (pompous, tediously dense). Limpid/lucid mean clear — opposites.

questions.subject: Text Completion
questions.q: Unlike his _____ predecessor, who decided everything alone, the new director consults the entire team.
questions.e: 'Unlike' + 'consults the entire team' contrasts with deciding alone: autocratic (ruling with absolute authority).

questions.subject: Text Completion
questions.q: The theory remains _____, supported by elegant mathematics but not yet by any direct observation.
questions.e: 'Supported by mathematics but not yet by direct observation' = still speculative (based on conjecture, not yet confirmed).

questions.subject: Text Completion
questions.q: His _____ memory for faces made him invaluable at conferences, where he greeted hundreds by name.
questions.e: 'Greeted hundreds by name' requires a large-capacity memory: capacious. (Tenacious = persistent — wrong context.)

questions.subject: Text Completion
questions.q: The play's second act was widely judged _____, a tedious stretch that added nothing to the story.
questions.e: 'A tedious stretch that added nothing' defines the blank: superfluous (unnecessary).

questions.subject: Text Completion
questions.q: Far from discouraging him, the rejection only _____ his determination to succeed.
questions.e: 'Far from discouraging' signals the opposite of dampened/stifled/shattered: whetted (sharpened, stimulated — as appetite).

questions.subject: Text Completion
questions.q: The historian's account is admirably _____, giving equal weight to evidence that supports and undermines her thesis.
questions.e: 'Equal weight to evidence that supports and undermines' = dispassionate (impartial, not influenced by strong feeling).

questions.subject: Text Completion
questions.q: The CEO's management style was (i)_____ rather than (ii)_____, favoring quiet consensus over dramatic confrontation.
questions.e: The sentence defines style as 'quiet consensus over dramatic confrontation' — so (i) = conciliatory and (ii) = abrasive, the contrasted term.

questions.subject: Text Completion
questions.q: The artist's early work was (i)_____ and experimental, while her later paintings became (ii)_____ and conventional.
questions.e: 'While' contrasts early vs late: early = audacious (bold), late = restrained. The 'conventional' tag confirms the second blank.

questions.subject: Text Completion
questions.q: The witness's testimony was (i)_____; far from clarifying events, it was so (ii)_____ that the jury grew more confused.
questions.e: 'Far from clarifying' contrasts with the first blank, and 'so... that the jury grew more confused' defines the second: testimony meant to be lucid was actually convoluted.

questions.subject: Text Completion
questions.q: The reform was (i)_____ in scope yet (ii)_____ in effect, touching every department but changing little.
questions.e: 'Yet' contrasts scope and effect: (i) = sweeping (broad), (ii) = negligible, confirmed by 'touching every department but changing little.'

questions.subject: Text Completion
questions.q: Her prose is (i)_____ rather than (ii)_____: every sentence is polished, but none surprises.
questions.e: The colon defines it: polished but unsurprising = correct rather than inspired.

questions.subject: Text Completion
questions.q: The diplomat was (i)_____ in public but (ii)_____ in private, praising the treaty on camera while working to undermine it.
questions.e: 'Praising... while working to undermine it' = (i) laudatory in public, (ii) duplicitous in private.

questions.subject: Text Completion
questions.q: The discovery was (i)_____ greeted as a breakthrough, though later analysis showed the results to be (ii)_____.
questions.e: 'Though later analysis' contrasts the early reception with the verdict: initially (greeted as breakthrough) / spurious (false).

questions.subject: Text Completion
questions.q: The professor is (i)_____ with praise for students but (ii)_____ with criticism of colleagues, generous to one group and harsh to the other.
questions.e: 'Generous to one group and harsh to the other' defines the pair: lavish with praise, unsparing (severe) with criticism.

questions.subject: Text Completion
questions.q: The novel's hero is (i)_____ rather than (ii)_____: he does the right thing, but only after exhausting every selfish alternative.
questions.e: 'Does the right thing, but only after exhausting every selfish alternative' = reluctant rather than (genuinely) virtuous.

questions.subject: Reading Comprehension
questions.q:
Many early naturalists assumed the beaver's dam-building was a purely instinctive act, executed identically by every colony. Recent fieldwork has overturned this view. Researchers documenting dam construction across watersheds found striking local variation: in fast, rocky streams, beavers weave dense lattices of small branches anchored against boulders, while in slow, marshy water they build broad, low mounds of mud and sedge. Juveniles raised in one habitat and relocated to another adopt the local style within a single season, which rules out a rigid genetic program.

What the beavers appear to possess instead is a flexible problem-solving repertoire: a general drive to slow and deepen water, combined with trial-and-error learning about local materials. The 'instinct,' in other words, is not a blueprint but a goal.

The primary purpose of the passage is to
o: argue that beaver dam-building is learned rather than purely instinctive
describe the anatomy of the North American beaver
criticize early naturalists for poor observation
prove that beavers cannot adapt to new habitats
questions.e: The passage contrasts the old 'purely instinctive' view with evidence of local variation and learning, concluding the instinct is 'not a blueprint but a goal.'

questions.q:
It has long been known that sleep benefits memory, but the mechanism remained elusive until researchers began tracking individual neurons. In a series of experiments, rats learned a maze and then slept while electrodes recorded hippocampal activity. During slow-wave sleep, the exact neural firing sequences from the maze runs were replayed — compressed in time, and coordinated with activity in the cortex, the brain's long-term storage site.

Crucially, disrupting these replay events impaired next-day recall, while leaving the animals' other cognitive functions intact. The findings suggest that sleep does not merely rest the brain; it actively transfers the day's experiences into durable memory.

The experiments with rats are described primarily to
o: illustrate the neural mechanism behind sleep's benefit to memory
prove that rats dream about mazes
show that sleep impairs hippocampal function
argue that cortex activity is unnecessary for memory
questions.e: The experiments reveal replay of firing sequences during sleep coordinated with the cortex — the mechanism of memory consolidation.

questions.subject: Reading Comprehension
questions.q:
Cities are typically 2–5°C warmer than surrounding countryside, a phenomenon known as the urban heat island. The standard explanation blames dark, heat-absorbing surfaces: asphalt and rooftops soak up solar energy by day and release it at night. Yet a recent modeling study found that surface properties account for barely half the observed warming.

The remainder, the study argues, comes from the city's three-dimensional geometry. Tall buildings trap outgoing longwave radiation, bouncing it between facades in a radiative canyon effect, while reduced wind flow at street level suppresses convective cooling. Mitigation, the authors conclude, must address urban form — building spacing, orientation, and ventilation corridors — not just surface color.

According to the passage, the 'standard explanation' of urban heat islands
o: accounts for only about half the observed warming
was proposed by the modeling study
questions.e: The study 'found that surface properties account for barely half the observed warming' — the standard explanation is incomplete, not wrong.

questions.subject: Reading Comprehension
questions.q:
The near-absence of women from early histories of science was long treated as evidence of absence: few women did science, so few appeared in the record. Historians of the last forty years have dismantled this inference. They found women working as astronomical computers, botanical illustrators, and laboratory managers — roles that produced science but not authorship, since credit flowed to the male head of the household or institution.

The revision goes deeper than adding names. Because women's scientific labor clustered in observation, illustration, and data management, recovering it has forced a broader definition of what counts as scientific work — one that values the production of reliable data as highly as the publication of theory.

o: the lack of women in historical records meant few women did science
women's absence from laboratories proves their inability
questions.e: The passage says absence from histories 'was long treated as evidence of absence: few women did science, so few appeared in the record' — a faulty inference the historians dismantle.

Venice's survival as a living city — not merely an open-air museum — has become the central question of its politics. With a historic-centre population that has fallen below 50,000 while annual visitors exceed 20 million, the arithmetic of overtourism seems inexorable: housing converts to short-term rentals, everyday shops yield to souvenir stands, and the young leave for the mainland.

Yet the narrative of inevitable decline misses countervailing forces. Strict rental regulations introduced in recent years have slowed the conversion of housing stock; a long-delayed entry fee for day-trippers, finally implemented, gives the city a lever — however modest — over visitor flows. The deeper question is what 'survival' means. If it means a city frozen at some imagined equilibrium, Venice is already lost. If it means a place that continues to adapt — as it has for a millennium, from maritime empire to tourist icon — then the current crisis is less an ending than another transformation, albeit one whose outcome remains genuinely uncertain.

o: qualify a pessimistic narrative about Venice with countervailing evidence
promote Venice as a tourist destination
argue that tourism should be banned in Venice
prove that Venice's population is growing
questions.e: The passage presents the overtourism 'arithmetic' then argues the 'narrative of inevitable decline misses countervailing forces' — qualifying pessimism.

questions.subject: Reading Comprehension
questions.q:
Coral reefs occupy less than 0.1% of the ocean floor yet sustain roughly a quarter of marine species — a productivity paradox that puzzled Darwin himself. The resolution lies in ruthless recycling: in nutrient-poor tropical waters, corals and their symbiotic algae pass nitrogen and phosphorus back and forth in a near-closed loop, wasting almost nothing. The reef is less a place than a process — an engine for concentrating scarcity into abundance.

That engine is now seizing up. When ocean temperatures exceed seasonal norms by even 1–2°C, corals expel their algal partners — the whitening known as bleaching. A bleached coral is not dead, but starving; if temperatures fall quickly, the partnership can resume, but prolonged heat kills. Three global bleaching events in the last three decades have killed roughly half the shallow-water corals of the Great Barrier Reef.

Restoration science has responded with techniques that would have seemed fanciful a generation ago: selective breeding for heat tolerance, probiotic treatments for coral microbiomes, and even the seeding of reefs with laboratory-grown larvae. Whether these interventions can scale to entire reef systems remains doubtful — the honest assessment is that they buy time rather than deliver salvation. The decisive variable, researchers agree, is the trajectory of ocean warming itself.

The 'productivity paradox' (paragraph 1) refers to
o: reefs supporting vast biodiversity despite occupying tiny, nutrient-poor areas
questions.e: 'Less than 0.1% of the ocean floor yet sustain roughly a quarter of marine species' in 'nutrient-poor tropical waters' — the paradox, resolved by recycling.

questions.e: 'Hesitant to cite it' = dubious (doubtful) origin.

questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.q: Using the root 'bene-' (good), what does 'benevolent' most nearly mean?
questions.e: 'Bene-' = good + 'vol' (wish) = wishing good: well-meaning and kindly.

questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.q: Using the prefix 'mal-' (bad), what does 'malinger' most nearly mean?
o: to pretend illness to avoid work
questions.e: 'Mal-' = bad; to malinger is to pretend to be ill to shirk duty.

questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.q: Using the root 'loqu' (speak), what does 'loquacious' most nearly mean?
questions.e: 'Loqu' = speak; loquacious = very talkative.

questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.q: Using the root 'path' (feeling), what does 'antipathy' most nearly mean?
questions.e: 'Anti-' (against) + 'path' (feeling) = feeling against: deep dislike.

questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.q: Using the root 'scrib/script' (write), what does 'proscribe' most nearly mean?
questions.e: 'Pro-' (forward, publicly) + 'scrib' = to write forth against: to forbid, outlaw.

questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.q: Using the root 'greg' (flock), what does 'egregious' most nearly mean?
questions.e: 'E-' (out of) + 'greg' (flock) = standing out from the flock — now meaning remarkably bad.

questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.q: Using the root 'ver' (true), what does 'verisimilitude' most nearly mean?
questions.e: 'Ver' (true) + 'simil' (like) = the likeness of truth: appearing true or real.

questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.q: Using the prefix 'circum-' (around), what does 'circumspect' most nearly mean?
questions.e: 'Circum-' (around) + 'spect' (look) = looking around carefully: cautious, wary.

questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.q: Using the root 'mit/miss' (send), what does 'remit' most nearly mean?
questions.e: 'Re-' (back) + 'mit' (send) = send back — e.g., remit payment.

questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.q: Using the root 'phil' (love), what does 'philanthropy' most nearly mean?
o: love of humanity shown through charity
questions.e: 'Phil' (love) + 'anthropos' (human) = love of humankind, expressed in charitable acts.

questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.q: Using the prefix 'anted-' , what does 'antediluvian' most nearly mean?
questions.e: 'Ante-' (before) + 'diluvium' (flood) = from before the (biblical) flood: absurdly antiquated.

questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.q: Using the root 'luc/lum' (light), what does 'pellucid' most nearly mean?
questions.e: 'Per-' (through) + 'luc' (light) = letting light through: transparently clear.

questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.q: Using the root 'mort' (death), what does 'moribund' most nearly mean?
questions.e: 'Mort' = death; moribund = on the point of death, in terminal decline.

questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.q: Using the prefix 're-' (back), what does 'recalcitrant' most nearly mean?
questions.e: 'Re-' (back) + 'calcitrare' (to kick) = kicking back: resisting authority.

questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.q: Using the root 'dict' (speak), what does 'malediction' most nearly mean?
questions.e: 'Male-' (bad) + 'dict' (speak) = evil speech: a curse.

questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.q: Using the root 'fac/fic' (make, do), what does 'munificent' most nearly mean?
questions.e: 'Muni-' (public duty/gift) + 'fic' (make) = making lavish gifts: extremely generous.

questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.q: Using the root 'spect' (look), what does 'retrospective' most nearly mean?
questions.e: 'Retro-' (back) + 'spect' (look) = looking back.

questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.q: Using the root 'tempor' (time), what does 'extemporaneous' most nearly mean?
questions.e: 'Ex-' (out of) + 'tempor' (time) = out of the moment: improvised, unprepared.

questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.q: Using the root 'voc' (call, voice), what does 'vociferous' most nearly mean?
questions.e: 'Voc' (voice) + 'fer' (carry) = carrying voice loudly: clamorous.

questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.q: Using the prefix 'super-' (above), what does 'supercilious' most nearly mean?
questions.e: 'Super-' (above) + 'cilium' (eyebrow) = raising eyebrows at others: arrogantly disdainful.

questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.q: Using the root 'doc' (teach), what does 'doctrinaire' most nearly mean?
questions.e: 'Doc' (teach) + doctrine = one who applies doctrine inflexibly.

questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.q: Using the prefix 'ob-' (against), what does 'obstreperous' most nearly mean?
questions.e: 'Ob-' (against) + 'strepere' (to roar) = roaring against control: unruly.

questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.q: Using the root 'ven/vent' (come), what does 'contravene' most nearly mean?
questions.e: 'Contra-' (against) + 'ven' (come) = to come against: to violate a law or rule.

questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.q: Using the prefix 'trans-' (across), what does 'transient' most nearly mean?
questions.e: 'Trans-' (across) + 'ire' (go) = going across, passing through: fleeting.

questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.q: Using the root 'jud/jur' (judge, law), what does 'adjudicate' most nearly mean?
questions.e: 'Ad-' (toward) + 'jud' (judge) = to act as judge: to settle judicially.

questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.q: The word 'enervate' looks like 'energize' but means:
questions.e: Classic GRE trap: enervate = to deprive of force or vitality (e- + nerves, unstringing).

questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.q: The word 'flag' as a verb on the GRE most often means:
questions.e: Second-meaning word: 'his energy flagged' = weakened.

questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.q: The word 'check' as a verb on the GRE most often means:
questions.e: Second-meaning word: 'checked his anger' = restrained it.

questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.q: The word 'qualify' on the GRE often means:
o: to limit or modify a statement
questions.e: Second-meaning word: 'she qualified her praise' = limited it.

questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.q: The word 'pedestrian' as an adjective on the GRE most often means:
questions.e: Second-meaning word: pedestrian prose = unimaginative, commonplace.

Honeybees communicate the location of food through the waggle dance — a figure-eight pattern whose angle relative to vertical encodes the sun's bearing and whose duration encodes distance. For decades this was considered a fixed, symbolic code. But recent experiments reveal a social dimension: experienced foragers adjust their dances based on the colony's needs, dancing more vigorously for scarce, high-quality sources and suppressing dances for mediocre ones.

Even more striking, novice bees that follow dances do not blindly obey. They integrate dance information with their own exploratory flights and with olfactory cues from returning foragers, sometimes ignoring dances that point to depleted patches. The waggle dance, it turns out, is less a set of orders than a contribution to a collective deliberation — one vote among many in the colony's foraging decisions.

questions.subject: Reading Comprehension
questions.q:
The placebo effect — improvement from an inert treatment — was long dismissed as mere gullibility. Modern neuroimaging has rehabilitated it: placebo analgesia triggers the release of endogenous opioids, and the effect can be blocked by naloxone, an opioid antagonist. The patient's expectation, it seems, is itself a pharmacological event.

This creates an ethical puzzle. If belief heals through real neurochemistry, is prescribing a placebo deception or treatment? Most ethicists draw a line at lying: open-label placebos — honestly described as inactive — still produce significant effects, suggesting that the ritual of treatment, not just deception, drives the benefit.

The author's attitude toward the traditional dismissal of placebos is
questions.e: 'Long dismissed as mere gullibility' vs 'Modern neuroimaging has rehabilitated it' — the dismissal was wrong.

capsules.subject: GRE
capsules.title: GRE General Test: structure and scoring
capsules.body: The GRE General Test has three sections — Analytical Writing (0-6), Verbal Reasoning and Quantitative Reasoning (130-170 each) — giving a total score range of 260-340, plus a 0-6 Analytical Writing score. The shorter test (about 1 hour 58 minutes) uses section-level adaptation: performance in the first operational section determines the difficulty of the second.

capsules.title: GRE vs GMAT Focus: which test for 2026–27?
